r20.text: The **phonological similarity effect** is the finding that people recall a list **worse when its items sound alike** than when they sound different. Since the sound is what matters, **acoustic similarity effect** is arguably the better name.
children: People studied lists of items that sounded alike or sounded different, read them silently, and then recalled them.
The surprising part is that it still happens when people **read the items silently**, with no sound presented.

r20.text: Silent reading still producing it means people **recode what they see into a speech-based form**. If memory held only a visual code, the mix-ups would be between items that **look** alike, such as E and F, instead of items that **sound** alike.
children: This recoding is the basis of the **phonological loop**, a component of **working memory**.

r20.text: The loop has a **phonological store**, which briefly holds speech-based traces, and an **articulatory control process**, which converts visual input into a speech code and refreshes the traces.
children: **Articulatory suppression** keeps that control process busy, so visual items cannot be recoded.
In the suppression condition, participants kept their speech busy while studying a visually presented list.
With recoding blocked, visually presented lists that sound alike and lists that sound different are **recalled equally well**.

r21.text: Items that **sound alike** are harder to recall in a list than items that sound different: the **phonological similarity effect**, or more accurately the **acoustic similarity effect**.
children: People studied lists of items that sounded alike or sounded different, read them silently, and then recalled them.
It appears even when the list is **read silently**.

r21.text: The explanation is that people **convert what they see into a speech code**. A purely visual code would instead produce mix-ups between look-alikes such as E and F.
children: This is the foundation of the **phonological loop** of working memory.

r21.text: The loop pairs a **phonological store** for short-lived speech traces with an **articulatory control process** that recodes visual input and refreshes the traces.
children: In the suppression condition, participants kept their speech busy while studying a visually presented list.
Occupying that process (**articulatory suppression**) blocks recoding, and the sound-alike cost disappears for visually presented lists.

r22.text: The **phonological similarity effect**: a list of items that **sound alike** is recalled worse than a list of items that sound different, even when it is only read silently. Because sound is what matters, **acoustic similarity effect** is arguably the better name.
children: People studied lists of items that sounded alike or sounded different, read them silently, and then recalled them.

r22.text: The best interpretation is that people **recode visual input into a speech code**. A purely visual code would cause confusions between look-alikes such as E and F instead.
children: This recoding is the basis of the **phonological loop** in working memory.

r22.text: The loop's **phonological store** briefly holds speech-based traces, and its **articulatory control process** converts visual input to speech and refreshes the traces.
children: In the suppression condition, participants kept their speech busy while studying a visually presented list.
With **articulatory suppression** occupying that process, recoding is blocked and the sound-alike cost disappears for visually presented lists.

r20.text: The **neighborhood size effect** shows that **knowledge stored in long-term memory changes short-term memory performance**. A word's **neighborhood** is every word you can make by changing one letter (**orthographic**) or one sound (**phonological**).
children: Cat has many neighbors, such as bat, cot and can, so it is a **large neighborhood word**; hippopotamus has none, so it is a **small neighborhood word**.

r20.text: Roodenrys and colleagues (2002) found that in short-term memory tasks, **large neighborhood words are recalled better** than small neighborhood words.
children: People recalled lists of words in order in a standard short-term memory task, with some lists made of large neighborhood words and others of small neighborhood words.
So what a person knows about the language helps them hold words briefly.

r20.text: This causes trouble for **memory span**. If long-term memory affects it, span **cannot be a pure measure of short-term memory capacity**.

r21.text: How well a word is held in **short-term memory** depends on how many similar words exist, which is a **long-term memory** influence: the **neighborhood size effect**.
children: Neighbors are words one letter (orthographic) or one sound (phonological) away; cat has many (**large neighborhood**), hippopotamus has none (**small neighborhood**).

r21.text: **Large neighborhood words are recalled better** than small neighborhood words, so language knowledge is shaping short-term performance.
children: People recalled lists of words in order in a standard short-term memory task, with some lists made of large neighborhood words and others of small neighborhood words.

r21.text: As a result, **memory span** is not a clean measure of short-term capacity.

r22.text: Roodenrys and colleagues (2002) found that **long-term memory affects short-term recall**: words from a **large neighborhood** are recalled better than words from a **small neighborhood**.
children: A neighborhood is the set of words one letter (orthographic) or one sound (phonological) away; cat has many, hippopotamus has none.
People recalled lists of words in order in a standard short-term memory task, with some lists made of large neighborhood words and others of small neighborhood words.

r22.text: Stored knowledge of words therefore boosts performance on a short-term memory task.
Because of this, **memory span** is not a pure measure of short-term memory capacity.

r20.text: The **Brown-Peterson task** was designed to test what happens to information in **short-term memory** when it cannot be rehearsed. People studied a few consonants and then did a hard **distractor task**, counting backwards, which stopped them from rehearsing the letters.
children: Peterson and Peterson (1959) ran this task.

r20.text: The longer the distractor lasted, the **less likely people were to recall the letters**.
children: Counting backwards is very different from remembering letters, so the researchers judged **interference** an unlikely cause of the forgetting.
Recall was tested after distractor periods of different lengths.

r20.text: Their conclusion was that **short-term memory (STM)** holds information only briefly, and that without rehearsal the information is lost through **decay**.
children: Decay is the researchers' own conclusion; the results have also been given an alternative explanation.

r21.text: In the **Brown-Peterson task**, people study a few letters and then do a **distractor task**, such as counting backwards, that stops rehearsal.
children: The longer the distraction, the **worse the recall**.
Recall was tested after distractor periods of different lengths.

r21.text: Counting is so unlike remembering letters that **interference** seemed an unlikely cause of the forgetting.
The conclusion was that **short-term memory (STM)** holds information only briefly and loses it through **decay** unless it is rehearsed.
children: That is the researchers' conclusion, and an alternative explanation of the results exists.

r22.text: In the **Brown-Peterson task**, people studied consonants and then counted backwards, a **distractor task** that blocked rehearsal. Peterson and Peterson (1959) found that the longer the distraction, the **worse the recall**.
children: Recall was tested after distractor periods of different lengths.

r22.text: Counting is so unlike remembering letters that they judged **interference** an unlikely cause.
children: They concluded that **short-term memory (STM)** holds information only briefly and loses it through **decay** unless it is rehearsed.

r22.text: Decay is the researchers' conclusion, not the only possible reading; an alternative explanation of the results has been offered.

r20.text: The **modality effect** is a better memory for the **last one or two items** of a list when the list is **heard** than when it is read silently.
children: The same kind of list was either heard or read silently (or lip-read or mouthed) and then recalled.
It also appears for lists that are **lip-read** or **silently mouthed**, so it is not only about hearing.

r20.text: These findings strongly influenced the idea of **sensory memory**, a back-up store that holds **raw, unanalyzed sensory input** and can improve recall when that information is useful.
The favored explanation, from Neath and Surprenant (2003), is that **hearing provides an additional type of information** compared with reading.
children: When recalling the last items, you do better if you also have information about **how the list sounded**.

r21.text: Hearing a list gives better memory for its **final one or two items** than reading it silently: the **modality effect**.
children: The same kind of list was either heard or read silently (or lip-read or mouthed) and then recalled.
Lip-read or mouthed lists give the same benefit.

r21.text: The effect pushed theories toward **sensory memory**, a back-up store of **raw, unanalyzed input** that helps when that information is useful.
The favored account is that hearing supplies **extra information about how the items sound**, and that supports the end of the list.

r22.text: The **modality effect** is an advantage for the **last one or two items** of a list that is **heard** over one read silently, and it also shows up for lip-read or silently mouthed lists.
children: The same kind of list was either heard or read silently (or lip-read or mouthed) and then recalled.

r22.text: It strongly shaped ideas about **sensory memory**, a back-up store of **raw, unanalyzed sensory input** that can help recall.
Neath and Surprenant (2003) favor the explanation that **hearing adds a further kind of information**, how the list sounds, which helps the final items.

r20.text: Early work found that people could report only a small part of a brief display. Sperling (1960) suggested this limit came from **recall**, not from perception.
children: He used the **partial-report** method, in which a cue given after the display tells observers which part to report.

r20.text: When the cue came **right after the display disappeared**, observers reported the cued part almost perfectly, whichever part it was.
children: So a **sensory (iconic) store** briefly held nearly a complete copy of the display.

r20.text: The real limit is the **time needed to report**, because the store fades while the observer is reporting.
children: When the cue was **delayed**, performance fell back toward the usual limit, which shows how **briefly** the store lasts.

r21.text: What limits report from a brief glance is **recall**, not perception: observers see far more than they can report.
The evidence is **partial report**. A cue to one part of the display just after it vanishes lets that part be reported almost perfectly, whichever part it is.
children: Observers briefly saw a display and were cued, after it vanished, to report only one part of it.
So a **sensory (iconic) store** briefly holds almost everything that was seen.

r21.text: Delay the cue and the advantage fades, so the store is **very short-lived**. The bottleneck is the **time it takes to report**, during which items fade.

r22.text: Sperling (1960) argued that the limit on reporting a brief display is on **recall**, not perception.
His **partial-report** method cued observers to one part of the display just as it vanished, and whichever part was cued came out nearly intact.
children: Observers briefly saw a display and reported only the part they were cued to, at different delays after it vanished.
That implies a **sensory (iconic) store** briefly held almost the whole display.

r22.text: A delayed cue lost the advantage, so the store **fades quickly**, and full report is limited because items disappear **while being reported**.

r20.text: The **position error effect** concerns memory for **order** as well as for items, such as the digits of a phone number. Most of the time an item is **recalled in its correct position**.
children: When a mistake is made, it is **systematic**, not random.
People recalled lists in order, and each recalled item's position was compared with its true position.

r20.text: A misplaced item most likely comes out in an **adjacent position**: an item that is not recalled third is probably recalled second or fourth, and rarely far from where it belongs.
This matters because **percent correct alone makes forgetting look like lost information**. In fact people still remember **roughly where the item belonged**.

r21.text: Memory for **order** is mostly right, and the mistakes follow a **pattern**: a misplaced item tends to land **next to its true position**, seldom far away.
children: People recalled lists in order, and each recalled item's position was compared with its true position.

r21.text: Because the errors are systematic, people keep **approximate position information**. Counting only **percent correct** treats a near miss as complete forgetting and hides this.

r22.text: Items are usually recalled in their **correct position**, and when they are not, the errors are **systematic**: the item lands in an **adjacent position**, so the third item is more likely to show up second or fourth than first or last.
children: People recalled lists in order, and each recalled item's position was compared with its true position.

r22.text: So forgetting a position is **not the same as losing the item**. Percent correct alone makes it look like lost information, but people retain **approximate position information**.

r20.text: The main theme is that **mental images behave like real images**. People report using mental images, such as when counting the windows in their home, but asking them to describe their images is unreliable, since it is impossible to tell whether the images differ or only the descriptions do.
children: So researchers use **tasks that require imagery** and vary one critical part of the task, which lets them work out objectively what images are like.

r20.text: Shepard and Metzler (1971) showed people two block shapes and asked whether they were the **same shape or mirror images**, with one shape turned relative to the other. People said they **mentally rotated** one shape to match the other.
children: The **larger the turn, the longer the response**, and the extra time grew at a **constant rate**.

r20.text: So rotating a mental image takes time, just as turning a real object does, which suggests **mental images are much like real images**.
children: This finding influenced **theories of mental representation**.

r21.text: Reports about our own mental images are a poor guide, because there is no way to tell whether the **images** differ or only the **descriptions** do. So tasks are used that force imagery and show it in behavior.
In the rotation task, people judged whether two block shapes were the **same or mirror images** when one was turned, and said they **mentally rotated** one to match the other.
children: The **bigger the turn, the longer the judgment**, rising at a **constant rate**.

r21.text: Rotating an image takes time, as with a real object, so **mental images are much like real images**, an idea that shaped **theories of mental representation**.

r22.text: Descriptions of mental images are unreliable, so imagery is studied with tasks that require it. Shepard and Metzler (1971) had people judge whether two block shapes were the **same or mirror images** when one was turned; people said they **mentally rotated** one shape to match the other.
children: The **bigger the turn, the longer the judgment**, and the extra time rose at a **constant rate**.

r22.text: Rotating an image takes time, as turning a real object does, which suggests **mental images are much like real images**.
The result influenced **theories of mental representation**.

r20.text: The main theme is that people judge probability with **heuristics**, which **trade accuracy for speed**. Heuristics are usually good enough day to day, but they can lead to **incorrect judgments**.
children: Tversky and Kahneman (1983) showed that people's estimates of probability often differ greatly from objective probability.

r20.text: A striking example is the **conjunction fallacy**: judging that **A and B together are more likely than A alone or B alone**.
children: By objective probability, a combination can **never be more likely than** either part on its own.

r20.text: Shafir, Smith and Osherson (1990) had people read short descriptions of a person and rate how likely it was that the person had certain professions or took part in certain activities. People sometimes rated the **combination as more likely than one part of it**.
children: This points to reliance on **heuristics** rather than the rules of probability.

r21.text: Probability judgments rely on **heuristics**: quick shortcuts that give up some accuracy. They usually work, but can produce **wrong judgments**, and estimates often stray far from the true probability.
The **conjunction fallacy** shows this: people say **A and B together** is more likely than A alone or B alone, although a combination is **never more likely than** either part.

When people read a short description of a person and rated the likelihood of professions or activities, they sometimes rated the **combination above a single part**, which indicates **heuristics**, not probability rules.

r22.text: Tversky and Kahneman (1983) showed that probability judgments often differ greatly from objective probability because people use **heuristics**, shortcuts that **trade accuracy for speed**.
The **conjunction fallacy** is judging **A and B together** more likely than A alone or B alone, though a combination is **never more likely than** either part.

Shafir, Smith and Osherson (1990) had people read a short description of a person and rate how likely certain professions or activities were. People sometimes rated the **combination above one part**, which points to **heuristics**, not probability rules.

r20.text: People find it hard to test an **abstract rule**. In the **Wason Selection Task**, the rule is "If a card has a D on one side, it has a 3 on the other side," and the job is to choose the cards that could show the rule is broken.
children: The correct cards are **D and 7**, because a D without a 3, or a 7 with a D behind it, would **falsify** the rule.
Most people pick D and 3, but the 3 can only **confirm** the rule, since the rule says nothing about what must be behind a 3.

r20.text: A rule with the same logic but familiar content, such as "If you borrow my car, you must fill up the gas tank," is **much easier**.
children: The right cards are **"borrowed car" and "empty gas tank,"** because those could reveal someone who borrowed the car and did not fill it.

r20.text: Wason and Shapiro (1971) compared abstract and thematic rules. People test a rule well when they have **relevant experience**.
children: With thematic rules they use experience; with abstract rules they must rely **solely on logic**.

r21.text: The card rule "If D on one side, then 3 on the other" is tested by the cards that could **break** it: **D and 7**.
children: People tend to turn D and 3, but the 3 can only **confirm** the rule, and they miss the 7, which could **falsify** it.

r21.text: Put the same logic in a familiar rule such as "If you borrow my car, you must fill up the tank," and it becomes **easy**: check the borrowed car and the empty tank.
**Relevant experience** makes a rule testable; without it, as with abstract rules, people must use **logic alone**.

r22.text: The **Wason Selection Task** asks which cards to turn over to test "If a card has a D on one side, it has a 3 on the other." Only **D and 7** could **falsify** it.
children: People commonly choose D and 3, but the 3 can only **confirm** the rule, and the 7 goes unchecked.

r22.text: A familiar rule with identical logic, "If you borrow my car, you must fill up the tank," is **far easier**: the borrowed car and the empty tank are the obvious cards to check.
Wason and Shapiro (1971) compared abstract with thematic rules and found that **relevant experience** lets people test a rule, whereas abstract rules leave only **logic**.

r20.text: The main theme is that **decisions are shaped by how a choice is framed**, not only by what the options are. People would like to weigh their options carefully, but many tendencies, called **framing effects**, push them in particular directions.
children: It is fairly easy to create a context in which people choose a particular option.

r20.text: In a **framing effect**, the **perceived context or wording of the choice** makes a big difference, even when the situations are **otherwise equivalent**.
children: Kahneman and Tversky (1982) summarized many framing effects.

r20.text: The same choice can be presented in **two different ways**, and people choose differently depending on the version.
children: **Gain wording** typically pushes people toward the **sure option** and **loss wording** toward the **gamble**, so the choice follows the framing and not the substance.

r21.text: **How a choice is framed shapes the decision**, not just the options themselves. Many such tendencies are called **framing effects**, and it is fairly easy to set up a context that steers people.
A **framing effect** means the **wording or context** changes the choice even though the situations are **otherwise equivalent**.
Show the same choice in **two different ways** and people choose differently: **gain wording** typically leads to the **sure option** and **loss wording** to the **gamble**.

r22.text: **How a choice is framed shapes the decision.** Kahneman and Tversky (1982) summarized many of these **framing effects**.
A framing effect is defined by the **wording or context** changing the choice even though the situations are **otherwise equivalent**.
Presented in **two different ways**, the same choice draws different answers: **gain wording** typically leads to the **sure option**, **loss wording** to the **gamble**.

r20.text: The main theme is that **intuition about probability is often wrong**, and the **Monty Hall 3 Door problem** is the classic example. A prize is behind one of three doors, you pick one, and the host, who is assumed to play fair and always do this, opens one of the other two doors to show **no prize**. Should you **stay or switch**?
children: Many people think it does not matter, which is **incorrect**.
The lab compares always switching, always staying and choosing at random over many plays.

r20.text: **The right choice is to switch.** Always switching wins about **two-thirds** of the time and always staying wins about **one-third**.
children: Most people miss this because they treat the two remaining doors as equally likely.

r20.text: Your first pick has a **1 in 3 chance** of being right, so there is a **2 in 3 chance** the prize is behind one of the other two doors.
children: When the host shows that one of those doors is empty, that whole **2 in 3 chance moves to the remaining door**, while your own door stays at 1 in 3.

r21.text: Three doors, one prize: you choose a door, then a host who always plays fair opens a different door with nothing behind it. **Switch**, because staying keeps your original odds and switching roughly doubles them.
children: The lab compares always switching, always staying and choosing at random over many plays.
Saying it makes no difference is the classic mistake.

r21.text: Your first guess is a long shot, and the host's reveal tells you nothing new about it. The combined chance held by the other two doors therefore **collapses onto the single door left closed**.
The error comes from seeing two doors and calling it a coin flip, which overlooks that the host **could not** open your door or the prize door.

r22.text: The **Monty Hall 3 Door problem** shows poor intuition about the probability of combinations of events. You pick a door, the host, who always plays fair this way, opens a no-prize door, and the best move is to **switch**.
children: The lab compares always switching, always staying and choosing at random over many plays.
Always switching wins about **two-thirds** of the time, always staying about **one-third**.

r22.text: The first pick keeps its **1 in 3** chance, so the other two doors together hold **2 in 3**. The reveal does not change your door's chance, so all **2 in 3** now sits behind the one remaining door.
Most people say the two doors are equally likely and that it makes no difference. That is **incorrect**.

r20.text: The main theme is that **risky choices depend on framing**: the way a choice is framed makes a big difference to the decision, even when the situations are **otherwise equivalent**.
children: This research looks at how the framing of a risky choice changes the decision.

r20.text: In this research people choose between a **guaranteed outcome** and a **gamble** with a stated chance of winning and a stated chance of losing.
children: The guaranteed outcome can be a gain or a loss, so researchers can see how **risk, stakes, and gain versus loss** affect the choice.

r20.text: People typically **avoid risk when the choice is about gains**, taking the sure thing, and **seek risk when the choice is about losses**, taking the gamble.
children: So risky decisions depend on how outcomes are **perceived**, not just on the objective odds.

r21.text: **Risky choices depend on how they are framed**, even when the situations are otherwise equivalent.
The standard setup offers a **sure outcome** against a **gamble**. The sure outcome can be a gain or a loss, which shows how **gain versus loss** changes the choice.
The typical pattern is **caution with gains** (take the sure thing) and **risk-taking with losses** (take the gamble). How the outcome is perceived matters, not just the odds.

r22.text: In a **framing effect** the same situation described differently draws a different choice, and risky decisions are a prime case.
Researchers set a **guaranteed outcome** against a **gamble** with stated chances of winning and losing, and make the guaranteed outcome either a gain or a loss to see what that does to the choice.
The typical result: with gains people **play it safe** and take the sure thing, while with losses they **gamble**. Perception of the outcome drives the decision, not only the odds.

r20.text: German and Defeyter (2000) asked whether young children show **functional fixedness**: being stuck on an object's **usual function**, so that a new use is slow or missed.
children: Problem solving normally improves with age, so younger children were expected to do worse.

In the task, a toy bear wanted to reach a toy on a high shelf, and the solution was to turn a box over and use it as a support. In one condition the box had first been shown being used as a container.
Children of 5, 6 and 7 did the task with or without that container demonstration (preutilization), and how long they took to solve it was measured.

r20.text: **Older children (6 and 7) were slower** to use the box as a support once its container use had been shown, while **5-year-olds were immune** and were even faster than the older children in that condition.
children: Without the container demonstration, children simply got better with age.

r20.text: The authors predicted this result: **younger children have a more fluid idea of function**, where any goal of the user can make an object's function.
children: Older children hold function more rigidly, so the demonstrated container use has to be **restructured** before the box can become a support.

r21.text: Young children may not get stuck on what an object is usually for, even though problem solving usually improves with age.
children: A toy bear needed a box turned over as a support to reach a toy on a high shelf, sometimes after the box had been shown as a container.
Children of 5, 6 and 7 did the task with or without that container demonstration, and how long they took to solve it was measured.

r21.text: Older children, 6 and 7, were **slowed by the container demonstration**. The **5-year-olds were not**, and solved faster than the older children in that condition.
children: With no demonstration, performance just improved with age.

r21.text: The likely reason is that **young children treat function as flexible**: whatever the user is trying to do can make something a tool.
children: Older children hold a use more firmly and must restructure the problem to see the box as a support.

r22.text: German and Defeyter (2000) tested whether children show **functional fixedness**, expecting younger children to do worse because problem solving improves with age.
children: Their box task had a toy bear reach a toy on a high shelf by using a box as a support, after the box was or was not shown as a container.
Children of 5, 6 and 7 took part, and how long they took to solve the task was measured.

r22.text: **Children of 6 and 7 were slowed** by the container demonstration, but **5-year-olds were immune** and solved faster than the older children in that condition.
children: Without the demonstration, children improved with age.

r22.text: The authors predicted the immunity because **young children have a more fluid idea of function**.
children: Older children hold function rigidly and must **restructure** the container use to see a support.

r20.text: The **irrelevant speech effect** is that speech you are told to ignore **impairs serial recall**, and **changing-state speech** (different syllables) hurts more than **steady-state speech** (one syllable repeated).
children: Accounts differ: the speech may corrupt **phonological traces**, changing sound may disrupt **order rehearsal** for any item, or sound may **capture attention**.
Leist and colleagues (2022) separated these accounts by testing **verbal** and **spatial** items in children and adults.
Third graders and adults remembered lists in order, made of words or of locations, while hearing speech to ignore (changing-state or steady-state) or silence.

r20.text: Speech **impaired verbal recall but not spatial recall**, in both children and adults.
children: Children were more impaired than adults relative to silence, and they were hurt by steady-state speech too, which adults were not.

r20.text: So the effect is **specific to verbal material**.
children: That is hard for the **attention-capture** and **changing-state** accounts, which predict disruption of spatial items too.
It fits **similarity-based interference** between the speech and the **phonological representations** of the list.

r21.text: Ignored speech still **disrupts recall of an ordered list**, and speech with changing syllables does more damage than one repeated syllable.
children: Theories disagree about why: it may corrupt sound-based memory traces, break up order rehearsal, or capture attention.

r21.text: The test was whether speech also disrupts memory for **locations**, in children and adults. It **did not**: only **word-like items** suffered.
children: Third graders and adults remembered lists in order, made of words or of locations, while hearing speech to ignore (changing-state or steady-state) or silence.
Children were hit harder than adults, even by repeated-syllable speech, although the extra cost of changing syllables was similar in both groups.

r21.text: That points to **interference with sound-based codes** and causes trouble for accounts that predict damage to any kind of item.

r22.text: Leist and colleagues (2022) asked why ignored speech disrupts serial recall, which **changing-state speech** (different syllables) does more than **steady-state speech** (one syllable repeated). The candidate causes were corrupted phonological traces, disrupted order rehearsal, and attention capture.
children: They tested **verbal** items and **spatial** items (locations) in children and adults.
Third graders and adults remembered lists in order, made of words or of locations, while hearing speech to ignore (changing-state or steady-state) or silence.

r22.text: Speech **did not disrupt spatial recall** in either children or adults, only verbal recall.
children: Children were more impaired than adults relative to silence, but the added cost of changing-state speech was about the same in both groups.

r22.text: Leist and colleagues concluded the effect is **specific to verbal material**, which challenges the **attention-capture** and **changing-state** accounts and fits **similarity-based interference** with phonological codes.

r20.text: **Cognitive offloading** is using actions such as writing things down to **reduce the mental demands** of a task.
children: Morrison and Richmond (2020) asked who offloads and whether it helps.
They expected people with **lower working memory capacity** to offload more.
People heard lists of letters of several lengths; on some trials they could write the letters down, and on others they had to rely on memory alone.

r20.text: **Offloading improved memory**, especially at **high loads** beyond short-term memory capacity, and people **offloaded more as the load grew**.
**Memory ability did not predict who offloaded**, and capacity did not predict the benefit either.
children: So offloading **may be a compensatory strategy** that helps across a wide range of memory ability.

r21.text: Writing things down is a way of **taking load off memory**.
children: The question was whether people use it when they most need it, and whether it works.

r21.text: When lists got longer than memory can hold, people **used the notepad more and remembered more** because of it.
children: People heard lists of letters of several lengths; on some trials they could write the letters down, and on others they had to rely on memory alone.

r21.text: The expected link to **poor memory ability did not appear**: weaker and stronger memories offloaded alike, and gained alike.
children: That suggests offloading **may help people of many abilities**.

r22.text: Morrison and Richmond (2020) studied **cognitive offloading**, using actions such as writing things down to reduce a task's mental demands, and tested whether people with weaker working memory offload more.
children: People heard lists of letters of several lengths; on some trials they could write the letters down, and on others they had to rely on memory alone.

r22.text: Offloading helped most at **high loads**, and people offloaded more as the load rose.
Memory ability did **not** predict who offloaded, and ability did not predict the benefit, so offloading **may be a compensatory strategy** across abilities.

r20.text: In the **bat-and-ball problem**, a bat and ball cost $1.10 together and the bat costs $1.00 more than the ball.
children: The intuitive answer is **10 cents**, but then the bat is only 90 cents more.
The correct answer is **5 cents**: ball x, bat x plus $1.00, so x is 5 cents.

r20.text: One account of the error is **unconscious attribute substitution**: reasoners neglect 'more than' and answer an easier question.
children: Support for it came from incorrect reasoners being **less confident** on the standard problem than on a control without 'more than', called **substitution sensitivity**.

r20.text: Hoover and Healy (2019), using matching problems, found that incorrect reasoners mostly **recalled and recognized 'more than'**, so it was not simply overlooked, but they apparently did not use its meaning.
children: Reasoners solved bat-and-ball style problems and were then tested on whether they remembered and recognized the phrase 'more than', even after other material had come in between.
Some reasoners did lose the phrase and many stayed very confident, so substitution may still occur for some.
Because they cannot be sure the error was substitution, they prefer the term **error sensitivity**.

r21.text: The **bat-and-ball puzzle** pulls people to answer 10 cents. Subtracting $1.00 from $1.10 leaves the bat only 90 cents more, so the right answer is **5 cents**.
One account says wrong answers come from **swapping in an easier question** without noticing.
children: Evidence for it: wrong reasoners were **less sure of themselves** than on a version without 'more than', as if they sensed a problem.

r21.text: Hoover and Healy (2019) found those reasoners often **still remembered the phrase 'more than'** but apparently did not use it, so the error may be **conscious** rather than hidden.
children: Reasoners solved bat-and-ball style problems and were then tested on whether they remembered and recognized 'more than', even after other material had come in between.
Others lost the phrase or stayed confident, so substitution can still happen for some.
Because the cause cannot be pinned down, they call the confidence drop **error sensitivity**.

r22.text: The **bat-and-ball problem**: 10 cents feels right, but 5 cents is correct because the bat must cost a dollar more than the ball.
One account of the error is **attribute substitution**: reasoners neglect 'more than' and answer an easier question.
children: Support for it: wrong reasoners were **less confident** on the standard problem than on a control version without 'more than' (**substitution sensitivity**).

r22.text: Hoover and Healy (2019) found wrong reasoners mostly **remembered 'more than'** but apparently did not use its meaning, evidence for a **conscious error process**.
children: Reasoners solved the problem and were then tested on whether they remembered and recognized 'more than', even after other material came in between.
Because some lost the phrase and many stayed confident, substitution may still occur for some.
They prefer **error sensitivity** because they cannot be sure the error was substitution.

r20.text: Giuliani and colleagues (2023) combined the **framing effect**, where people prefer the **sure option for gains** and the **risky option for losses**, with the **default effect**, a tendency to take the **preselected option**.
children: The Asian disease problem is the classic framing example: 'saved' wording favors the sure program and 'die' wording favors the risky one.
The two effects had mostly been studied separately.

r20.text: People made **life-or-death** and **financial** choices with **no default**, a **sure default**, or a **risky default**.
children: Each choice was worded as a gain or as a loss, and people chose in life-or-death and in financial scenarios.

They found a **classic framing effect** and **more risk taking when lives were at stake**, although lives concerned people elsewhere while the money was the participant's own, so involvement differed.
A **risky default raised risk taking**, a **sure default did not raise risk aversion**, and framing and default were **additive**.

r20.text: Afterward people said why they thought the option was preselected. Those who saw it as the **most rational choice** followed it most, **expert advice** left people indifferent, and **previous respondents or chance** went with rejecting it.
children: This question was exploratory and came after the choice, so beliefs may partly justify a choice already made.

r21.text: Two influences on choice were tested together: **wording** (people take the sure thing when outcomes are gains and gamble when they are losses) and **defaults** (people drift to whatever is preselected).
When choices were about lives or about money, with the sure or the risky option preselected, **wording kept its usual effect** and the effects of wording and default simply **added up**.
children: Each choice was worded as a gain or as a loss, and people chose in life-or-death and in financial scenarios.
A **risky default pushed people toward risk**, while a **sure default did not make them more cautious** overall.
Risk was higher when lives were at stake, though involvement also differed from the money case.

r21.text: Afterward people said why they thought the option was preselected. Those who saw it as the **most rational choice** followed it most, **expert advice** left people indifferent, and **previous respondents or chance** went with rejecting it.
children: That was an after-the-fact, exploratory question, so beliefs may partly reflect justification of a choice already made.

r22.text: Giuliani and colleagues (2023) joined two influences on choice in one study: the **framing effect** (the sure option for gains, the risky option for losses) and the **default effect** (a tendency to take the preselected option).
children: People made life-or-death and financial choices with no default, a **sure default**, or a **risky default**.
Each choice was worded as a gain or as a loss, and people chose in life-or-death and in financial scenarios.

r22.text: They found a **classic framing effect** and more risk taking with lives than money, though the lives concerned people elsewhere and the money was the participant's own.
children: A **risky default raised risk taking** while a **sure default did not raise risk aversion** overall.
Framing and default effects were **additive**.

r22.text: In an exploratory question after the choice, belief in the default as **most rational** went with following it most, **expert advice** with indifference, and **previous respondents or chance** with rejection.
children: Beliefs may partly be justification of a choice already made.

r20.text: Albert, Chein and Steinberg (2013) reviewed why adolescents take more risks in real life although they **reason about risk as well as adults in the lab**.
children: Their answer is the **peer context**: adolescents take more risks with peers present than alone, and adults do not.
Peers prime the **reward system** (ventral striatum, orbitofrontal cortex) while the **cognitive-control system** (lateral prefrontal cortex) matures slowly, a **maturational gap**.

r20.text: Chein and colleagues (2011) scanned people playing a **driving game** **alone** or **watched by friends** in another room, with no interaction during play.
children: Adolescents took significantly more risks when watched, though the age-by-context difference on behavior was not itself significant in this small sample.
The game was a Stoplight driving game in which going was the risky decision.
The **ventral striatum and orbitofrontal cortex** were more active when friends watched, and this went with risky decisions.

r20.text: **Cognitive-control regions** were less engaged in adolescents than adults but did **not change with peers**, so the authors concluded the peer effect works mainly through **reward circuitry**, though the review points out that the two systems influence each other.
children: People less resistant to peer influence showed a larger reward response; peers also raise preference for **immediate rewards**, even when only believed to be watching.

r21.text: Teens reason about risk about as well as adults when alone, so the extra real-world risk is attributed to **the social setting**.
children: Teens take more risks with friends present than alone, and adults do not.

r21.text: In a brain-scan driving game, teens played alone or with friends **watching from another room** and not interacting.
children: When watched, **reward areas became more active** in teens and this went with riskier choices, even though the behavior gap between age groups was not itself firm in a small sample.
The game was a Stoplight driving game in which going was the risky decision, scanned with fMRI.

r21.text: **Control areas did not change with an audience**, so the effect seems to come mainly from a **stronger reward response** rather than weaker self-control, although the review points out that the two systems interact.
children: Peers also push toward immediate rewards, even when only believed to be watching.

r22.text: Albert, Chein and Steinberg (2013) point to the peer context: adolescents, but not adults, take more risks with peers than alone.
children: Their model is a **maturational gap** between a peer-primed **reward system** and a slowly maturing **cognitive-control system**.

r22.text: Chein and colleagues (2011) scanned a **driving game** played alone or watched by friends, and found adolescents took significantly more risks when watched, though the age-by-context difference on behavior was not itself significant in this small sample.
children: The task was a Stoplight driving game in which going was the risky decision, played in an fMRI scanner.
Reward regions (**ventral striatum, orbitofrontal cortex**) were more active in adolescents when peers watched, going with risky decisions.

r22.text: **Cognitive-control regions did not change with peers**, so the authors concluded the effect works mainly through **reward circuitry**, though the review points out that the two systems interact.
children: Peers also raise preference for immediate rewards, even when only believed present.
